headlines.title: Crash sparks fire at CaliBunga Waterpark in San Jose
headlines.description: A crash sparked a fire at CaliBunga Waterpark in San Jose on Saturday, the fire department said. Firefighters said around 4:40 p.m., a pickup truck crashed into a fence, caught fire and the flames spread to nearby vegetation. They asked the public to avoid the area. CaliBunga Waterpark, formerly known as Raging Waters, temporarily closed due to renovations and upgrades.

headlines.title: Apartment complex in San Francisco evacuated after lithium-ion battery fire
headlines.description: A six-story apartment complex in San Francisco’s South of Market neighborhood was evacuated Saturday after a lithium-ion battery caught fire. San Francisco firefighters responded to the fire in the 1000 block of Mission Street and began evacuating residents at about noon. The cause was determined to be a scooter with a lithium-ion battery that caught fire on the third story, according to the San Francisco Fire Department. The fire was extinguished in about 15 minutes and did not spread beyond the third floor. No injuries were reported.

headlines.title: Man dies after shooting in San Francisco
headlines.description: A man died after a shooting in San Francisco early Saturday morning, the police department said. Officers responded to the 900 block of Market Street regarding a shooting around 1 a.m., according to authorities. The man was taken to the hospital, where he was later pronounced dead, the police department said. Police said this remains an active investigation. They asked anyone with information to contact them at 415-575-4444 or text a tip to TIP411 and begin the message with SFPD.

headlines.title: Gabby Williams scores 19 as Valkyries rally from 16 down to beat Wings 77-73, reach WNBA semifinals
headlines.description: Gabby Williams scored 19 points and hit a go-ahead 17-footer with 1:17 remaining, and the Golden State Valkyries won a late replay review to finish a rally from 16 points down and beat the Dallas Wings 77-73 on Friday night in a wild deciding Game 3 of their first-round WNBA playoff series. With 13.1 seconds left and Golden State leading by one, Williams jumped back inbounds to corral her own miss on a play that was originally ruled Dallas’ ball, but Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase — who moments earlier had fallen to her knees on the sideline before being helped up — successfully challenged the call. Nakase walked off the court escorted by a member of her staff after the final buzzer, holding her face as the team celebrated at midcourt. Arike Ogunbowale knocked down an off-balance jumper with 3:13 to play that put Dallas up by five and finished with 30 points to follow up a 45-point performance in the Wings’ overtime win Wednesday night at home. Williams scored all but two of her points after halftime. Veronica Burton had 16 points, 10 rebounds and six assists. Burton’s layup with 8:19 to play pulled the Valkyries within 61-59, Williams hit two 3-pointers late in the third and they both willed Golden State into the best-of-five semifinals against the defending WNBA champion Las Vegas Aces. Game 1 is Sunday at rocking Ballhalla with the team’s deafening, violet-crazed home crowd at Chase Center. Tiffany Hayes scored 18 points off the bench, Kaila Charles hit a tying 3-pointer with 6:51 left and Kiah Stokes pulled down 13 rebounds. The second-seeded Valkyries won a playoff series for the first time. Last year, they became the first expansion team to reach the playoffs in its inaugural season. Paige Bueckers had 17 points with six assists but shot only 3 for 14 for Dallas, making all 10 of her free throws. The Valkyries missed three straight 3s and nine shots in a row overall to start the third quarter as Dallas used a 9-0 run to take its largest lead at 53-37. Golden State pulled within 59-54 heading into the final 10 minutes. Ogunbowale was 11 for 21 after scoring a playoff-record 45 points in the Wings’ 108-100 overtime win Wednesday night. That prompted Nakase to declare before the game: “We made a promise to ourselves we are going to play the best four quarters of our lives.” She said the Valkyries didn’t recognize themselves that game — even though the team had scored 100 or more points in the first two matchups, including 104-80 in the series opener last Sunday. ___ AP WNBA: https://apnews.com/hub/wnba-basketball

headlines.title: Man arrested following crime spree in San Mateo, police say
headlines.description: A man was arrested in connection with a hit-and-run that turned into a crime spree in San Mateo early Saturday morning, according to the police department. Officers responded to the 200 block of West 40th Avenue after receiving a report of a hit-and-run crash, authorities said. Police said they found the suspect vehicle, a Nissan Altima, abandoned nearby. Authorities said they later learned the Altima was stolen, but it hadn’t been reported as stolen. A witness identified the suspect as David Estrada, saying Estrada ran away from the area of the crash, according to police. Around 25 minutes later, police said they responded to the 300 block of 41st Avenue after a homeowner reported that Estrada had entered his home and was seen rummaging through a drawer. Authorities said Estrada fled after the homeowner confronted him. Police said Estrada had also entered and rummaged through a vehicle associated with the home before entering the home. Estrada was found inside another parked vehicle in the 3900 block of Fernwood Street, according to the police department. Authorities said the vehicle belonged to nearby residents who did not know Estrada and did not give him permission to be inside. Police said they determined the vehicle had also been rummaged through. During a search, authorities said they found brass knuckles with a window punch and switchblade knife attached in Estrada’s possession. During a neighborhood canvass, officials said they also discovered another vehicle partially blocking a roadway and driveway. They said Estrada was caught on surveillance video entering that vehicle and moving it from the driveway before abandoning it. Estrada was arrested and booked into the San Mateo County Jail, the police department said.

headlines.title: 1 dead following multi-vehicle crash on I-80 in Berkeley
headlines.description: A deadly crash involving multiple vehicles on Interstate 80 in Berkeley is under investigation, according to the California Highway Patrol. The collision was reported just before 3:30 p.m. Friday and shut down several lanes on westbound I-80 near the University Avenue exit. At least five vehicles were involved in the collision and one person was pronounced dead at the scene, CHP said. There was no estimated time lanes would reopen and motorists were encouraged to use alternate routes. headlines.title: Man arrested after stabbing in Brentwood
headlines.description: A man from Florida was arrested after allegedly stabbing another man in Brentwood on Friday night, according to the police department. Police said they received a report of a stabbing in the 2000 block of Elkins Way just before 8 p.m. At the scene, authorities say responding officers found the suspect, a 53-year-old man from Tallahassee, Florida. Police said they also found a man with several stab wounds to his lower torso. Officers provided medical aid to the victim, who was later taken to a local hospital for further treatment, according to authorities. Police said the suspect was taken into custody.

headlines.title: Man, woman dead after shooting at Oakland Hills home
headlines.description: A 61-year-old man and 63-year-old woman were found dead from apparent gunshot wounds outside their Oakland Hills home late Friday morning, according to police. Oakland and Berkeley police officers responded at about 10:45 a.m. to 499 Panoramic Way, not far from the University of California, Berkeley campus, to investigate reported gunshots, Oakland Police Department Assistant Chief Casey Johnson said. Officers found the man and woman suffering from apparent gunshot wounds outside the home. They both died at the scene, Johnson said. The man and woman appeared to be married and were residents at the home, according to Johnson. A firearm was recovered at the scene, Johnson said. It wasn’t immediately known if the shooting was a homicide or murder-suicide. “Everything’s a possibility until we can fully investigate this incident,” Johnson said. Johnson said there was no one in custody as of 1:30 p.m., adding that police were not looking for anyone at-large and that there was no threat to the surrounding neighborhood.

headlines.title: G7 nations will release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel fuel after prices soar
headlines.description: The Group of Seven wealthy democracies said Friday that they plan to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products in the coming weeks, starting with “substantial” amounts of diesel after the fuel recently hit record high prices in the United States. President Donald Trump said the diesel release would happen “immediately,” echoing a G7 promise to start “immediately” with a “frontloaded substantial release” of diesel within the next 20 days and the rest over four months. Trump and his Republican Party face pressure to address surging prices ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, and Trump announced the action Friday on social media. The president’s approval ratings on the economy hit a new low, according to an AP-NORC poll, as the Iran war and his trade battles have increased U.S. prices for oil and other goods. Gas prices in the U.S. and abroad have soared during the eight-month-long war, a cost Trump has repeatedly said is worth it for making sure Iran does not obtain nuclear weapons. The national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. was $6.37 on Friday, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22. Diesel prices have hit records in Europe, too. The release of diesel in Europe might mean less exports of diesel from the U.S., which could lower prices by 25-50 cents per gallon after a few weeks, said Michael Lynch, distinguished fellow at Energy Policy Research Foundation, a non-partisan research institution focused on energy and economics. Macron says the decision should bring down prices France holds the rotating presidency of the G7 group and made the announcement in a statement released after videoconference talks that Macron presided over. The G7 countries are Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the U.K. and the U.S., plus EU representation. The release follows on from a March announcement that International Energy Agency member countries would release 426 million barrels of oil and products to stabilize the oil market. European Union countries committed about 92 million barrels, a promise weighted toward refined products made from crude such as diesel. “This common decision and this unity should bring down prices,” Macron said. “The volumes we’re releasing should also add liquidity to the market and bring down prices.” In addition to the rise in the price of the crude oil from which diesel is made, other factors include the decision by Russia to ban exports due to Ukrainian drone strikes on its refineries. Europe does not import Russian diesel, but other buyers of Russian diesel such as Turkey and Latin American countries must now compete with Europe for available barrels. Meanwhile refined product shipments from the Persian Gulf producers have fallen due to war damage and blocked export routes. The statement pushed U.S. oil prices down 2% but “the impact was lessened by lack of clarity on an important question,” said Pavel Molchanov, investment strategy analyst at Raymond James. Is the 100 million barrels in addition to the amount already agreed in March, or “is this the final portion of the existing pledge?” he said. The G7 says export bans are off the table Some Republicans in the U.S. had called for Trump to ban U.S. exports of diesel to try to bring domestic prices down. But the G7 statement said the group agreed not to limit energy exports to each other. Oil market analysts warn a U.S. export ban could lower prices in the short term but eventually backfire by reducing supplies of gasoline since diesel output can’t be lowered without also cutting overall refinery production. Asked about a potential U.S. export ban on Friday, Trump said “we were never going to do it.” “We’re not going to be doing the export ban,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “We’re going to be doing what we’re supposed to do.” He added that Europe is making “a major world contribution, and so are we.” Experts say there are risks in the strategy The emergency release could also be a short-term fix with the potential to do long-term harm, said Jim Krane, energy research fellow at Rice University’s Baker Institute. “Draining stocks will reduce retail fuel prices for a while, at the cost of leaving Europe with less emergency cover,” Krane said. “At some point in the future Europe and the rest of the G7 will have to refill their strategic reserves. Normally they try to do this when prices are low. Nobody knows when that will happen. It’s a risk.” With two wars raging that involve attacks on refineries and exports, “it’s not the best time to be frittering away your emergency stocks — especially when there is no visibility on future prices or peace agreements,” Krane said. Trump had a conversation overnight with Macron about the need to address rising fuel prices and the availability of petroleum products, according to the French Embassy in the U.S. Macron on Friday then chaired the videoconference of G7 leaders to discuss the issue. Besides his call with Macron, Trump on Friday called in to the meeting with the G7 leaders to negotiate the release of the European diesel stockpiles, according to a White House official who was not authorized to speak publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity. Trump on Thursday embarked on what he said would be a 32-day marathon of rallies to try to bolster his party’s chances for keeping control of the U.S. House and Senate in the November elections. The president has grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a disconnect between his achievements and the public’s view of his work. This week he gave himself an A-plus for his work on the economy but said “we’re doing an extremely poor job of promotion.” ___ Leicester reported from Paris. AP writer Michelle L. Price contributed to this report. AP Business Writer David McHugh contributed from Frankfurt, Germany and Cathy Bussewitz contributed from New York.
headlines.source: COLLIN BINKLEY and JOHN LEICESTER | Associated Press

headlines.title: Volunteers needed for the ‘2026 Roadside Wildlife Count' project
headlines.description: The Environment American Research and Policy Center is looking for volunteers for a project aimed at protecting wildlife movement. It focuses on wildlife crossings, the overpasses and underpasses that help ensure that wildlife can find their habitats, prevent roadkill, and keep population numbers healthy. However, expanding roads and infrastructure have made it harder for mountain lions, deer, elk, and even threatened amphibians to keep their homes and access to resources. That’s why, starting Sunday until Oct. 11, volunteers are needed to help track wildlife by the road via an app in an effort to get more funding for wildlife crossings. According to a 2024 UC Davis Road Ecology Report, California roads with the highest consistent rates of wildlife-car crashes are 680 in Contra Costa and Alameda Counties, 280 on the Peninsula, and Highway 17 between San Jose and Santa Cruz. The Environment America Center says wildlife crossings are proven to reduce wildlife vehicle collisions by over 90%. Those who would like to volunteer and help spot the animals are encouraged to visit the Environment America website and search for the 2026 Roadside Wildlife Count.

headlines.title: San Jose pantry using sidewalk to hand out food facing city code violations
headlines.description: A San Jose food pantry said it might have to close after the city gave it an order to stop handing out food because it is blocking parts of a public sidewalk. The Lighthouse Food Rescue on north 17th Street has been put on notice. Code enforcement sent the nonprofit an email saying its use of the sidewalk to distribute food does not comply with current zoning rules. The city also says the farmer’s market style setup obstructs a public sidewalk and has given lighthouse 60 days to cease operations. The Lighthouse already faced a battle with the city during the COVID-19 pandemic over permits. But this time, the nonprofit might be forced to close. Dennis Grijalva is one of those in line preparing hours before opening the food pantry. “I mean, food prices have gone up and up and up and up. People’s salaries haven’t really changed. And those who haven’t it’s not enough to compensate for people’s food need,” Grijalva said. “We’re in a strange time right now where we feel there’s all this red tape in our nonprofit world. And doing a good deed today is just not easy,” president and CEO Pastor Ralph Olmos said. Lighthouse says it will fight city hall. The nonprofit’s lawyer sent a letter to the director of code enforcement, demanding a sit-down meeting. “I’ve reached out to our Code department to see if we can provide an extension to Lighthouse as they work to find a new location,” said San Jose Mayor Matt Mahan. “My team is also working to connect the Pastor with potential partners who may be able to store their resources temporarily while they find a more permanent solution. While we have to follow the law and zoning designations, we can do it with care and find compromises.”

headlines.title: Oakland's Skyline High cancels football season early due to player availability
headlines.description: Skyline High in Oakland is ending its varsity football season early after the school says it no longer has enough players available. Skyline High is the second East Bay school in the past week to cancel its season, partly due to player safety. The first school was Mount Diablo High. The school was supposed to play against Benicia High, but Mount Diablo High canceled its varsity season last week amid player safety concerns. “We had to scramble to fill our spot today to have a homecoming game and we’ve heard of other schools having to do the same,” Benicia High principal Brianna Kleinschmidt said. Skyline High did the same. The storied Oakland program, once led by the late John Beam, is canceling its season, citing injuries, transfers and other circumstances impacting player availability. In a statement, the principal wrote, “This is a decision we do not take lightly and it came after exhausting all other options.” The news came as a shock to many in the McClymonds crowd, since the school has been rivals with Skyline over the years. “It’s a shock really, because when I was growing up Skyline was the dominant force,” parent Laron Blackwell said. Leia Grew, a parent, agrees that player safety comes first. Her son even chose to wear a “guardian cap” over his helmet as an added layer of protection. “He’s the only one on the team that has one. I’m really happy he has it on, we do a lot of stretching. I think player safety is of big importance,” she said. Some head trauma experts can’t say whether head-injury concerns are driving high school players away from football, but what has changed is awareness. “The awareness of head injuries have gone up. More parents are seeking care when their kid gets injured,” UCSF neurological surgery assistant professor Dr. John Yue said. Looking ahead, Skyline says it will spend the rest of the school year recruiting more student athletes, with the goal of rebuilding its football program for next season.
